\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The measurement}

Abstract computation is modelled with great economy by a \emph{transition relation}: a set $\alpha$ of configurations and a binary relation $R \subseteq \alpha\times\alpha$, where $R\,a\,b$ means ``the machine may pass from $a$ to $b$ in one step''. Automata, rewriting systems, Kripke structures, Markov chain supports and abstract state machines are all instances.

Fix a state $a$ and make the crudest possible observation: for which $n$ can the machine, started at $a$, be at $a$ again after exactly $n$ steps? Write $\D(R,a) \subseteq \N$ for the answer, the \emph{degree monoid} of the state. This paper studies systematically what values it takes, which operations on machines it turns into which operations on numbers, and what it detects.

Three motivations: \emph{coarseness with completeness} (the observation discards almost everything, yet its range is exactly a well-understood algebraic lattice); \emph{behavioural robustness} (invariance under bisimulation); and \emph{discriminating power} (it separates deterministic from nondeterministic computation, absolutely and without resource bounds).

\subsection{Results}

Throughout, $\N = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$; a set $M \subseteq \N$ is an \emph{additive submonoid} if $0 \in M$ and $M + M \subseteq M$; $\langle S\rangle$ is the submonoid generated by $S$; and $n\N = \{0,n,2n,\dots\}$.

\begin{enumerate}
\item $\D(R,a)$ is an additive submonoid of $\N$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:monoid}).
\item Simulations increase the invariant; bisimulations preserve it (Theorems~\ref{thm:sim}, \ref{thm:bisim}).
\item $\D(R\times S,(a,b)) = \D(R,a)\cap \D(S,b)$ and $\D(R^{[k]},a) = (\D(R,a):k)$ (Theorems~\ref{thm:prod}, \ref{thm:rescale}).
\item Realisation: $\D(C_S,0) = \langle S\rangle$, so every additive submonoid of $\N$ occurs (Theorem~\ref{thm:real}, Corollary~\ref{cor:complete}).
\item Every additive submonoid occurs already on a finite state space (Theorem~\ref{thm:finite}).
\item Structure theory: divisibility by the period, eventual completeness, finiteness of gaps, dichotomy, and the synchronisation law (Section~\ref{sec:structure}).
\item Determinism forces $\D(R,a) = d\N$; gaps certify nondeterminism; no deterministic machine realises $\langle 2,3\rangle$; a live deterministic machine on $N$ states has period $\le N$ (Section~\ref{sec:det}).
\item For coprime $p,q>1$ the two-loop machine misses exactly $(p-1)(q-1)/2$ lengths, the largest being $pq-p-q$ (Section~\ref{sec:sylvester}).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Exact-length reachability and the degree monoid}

\begin{definition}[Iterated relation]
For $R$ on $\alpha$ define $R^{(n)}$, reachability in exactly $n$ steps, by
\[
  R^{(0)}\,a\,b \iff a = b, \qquad R^{(n+1)}\,a\,c \iff \exists b,\; R\,a\,b \wedge R^{(n)}\,b\,c .
\]
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Concatenation law]\label{lem:concat}
For all $m,n,a,c$: $R^{(m+n)}\,a\,c \iff \exists b,\; R^{(m)}\,a\,b \wedge R^{(n)}\,b\,c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $m$. For $m = 0$ both sides say $R^{(n)}\,a\,c$ (take $b = a$). For the step, unfold $R^{(m+1+n)}\,a\,c$ as $\exists x,\ R\,a\,x \wedge R^{(m+n)}\,x\,c$, apply the induction hypothesis to the tail and reassociate.
\end{proof}

Concatenation is the engine of the theory: it makes the return-length set additively closed and, read backwards, allows a long loop to be split at any intermediate time.

\begin{definition}[Degree monoid]
$\D(R,a) = \{\, n \in \N : R^{(n)}\,a\,a \,\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monoid law]\label{thm:monoid}
$\D(R,a)$ is an additive submonoid of $\N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$0 \in \D(R,a)$ since $R^{(0)}\,a\,a$ is $a = a$. If $m,n \in \D(R,a)$ then Lemma~\ref{lem:concat} with $b := a$ gives $R^{(m+n)}\,a\,a$.
\end{proof}

No closure under subtraction is asserted, and $2,3 \in \D(R,a)$ does not force $1 \in \D(R,a)$. That failure is the phenomenon of \emph{gaps}, shown in Section~\ref{sec:det} to be exactly the trace of nondeterminism.

\begin{example}\label{ex:basic}
(i) The empty relation gives $\D = \{0\}$. (ii) The total relation gives $\D = \N$. (iii) A directed $n$-cycle gives $\D = n\N$. (iv) Two loops of lengths $2$ and $3$ glued at $a$ give $\D = \langle 2,3\rangle = \{0,2,3,4,\dots\}$, which omits $1$.
\end{example}

\section{Functoriality and algebraic laws}

\begin{theorem}[Simulation monotonicity]\label{thm:sim}
If $f:\alpha\to\beta$ satisfies $R\,a\,b \Rightarrow S\,(fa)\,(fb)$, then $\D(R,a) \subseteq \D(S,fa)$ for all $a$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $n$, $R^{(n)}\,a\,b$ implies $S^{(n)}\,(fa)\,(fb)$; take $b = a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bisimulation invariance]\label{thm:bisim}
Let $f:\alpha\to\beta$ be injective with $R\,a\,b \iff S\,(fa)\,(fb)$, and suppose that whenever $S\,(fa)\,y$ holds, $y$ lies in the image of $f$. Then $\D(R,a) = \D(S,fa)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
``$\subseteq$'' is Theorem~\ref{thm:sim}. For ``$\supseteq$'', show by induction on $n$: if $S^{(n)}\,(fx)\,y$ then $y = fz$ for some $z$ with $R^{(n)}\,x\,z$. The first step out of $fx$ lands in the image, say at $fu$, and reflects to $R\,x\,u$; recurse from $u$. With $y = fa$, injectivity gives $z = a$.
\end{proof}

Thus the invariant sees only step behaviour, not presentation. By Theorem~\ref{thm:sim} it is monotone under abstraction, so \emph{non-membership} is sound to verify on an over-approximation.

\begin{definition}
The \emph{synchronous product} $R \times S$ on $\alpha\times\beta$ is given by $(R\times S)\,(a,b)\,(a',b') \iff R\,a\,a' \wedge S\,b\,b'$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Product law]\label{thm:prod}
$\D(R\times S,(a,b)) = \D(R,a) \cap \D(S,b)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $n$, $(R\times S)^{(n)}\,p\,q \iff R^{(n)}\,p_1\,q_1 \wedge S^{(n)}\,p_2\,q_2$; specialise $p = q = (a,b)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}
For $k\in\N$ let $R^{[k]}$ denote $R^{(k)}$ viewed as a one-step relation: $k$ old steps per new tick.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Rescaling law]\label{thm:rescale}
$n \in \D(R^{[k]},a) \iff kn \in \D(R,a)$; equivalently $\D(R^{[k]},a) = (\D(R,a):k) := \{n : kn \in \D(R,a)\}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $n$, $(R^{(k)})^{(n)} = R^{(kn)}$, the step case being Lemma~\ref{lem:concat} applied to $k + kn$.
\end{proof}

Rescaling can destroy gaps: $(\langle 2,3\rangle : 2) = \N$, since $2n \in \langle 2,3\rangle$ for every $n$. Section~\ref{sec:future} turns this observation into a research programme.

\section{The Realisation Theorem}

\begin{definition}[Chain machine]
For $S \subseteq \N$ define $C_S$ on the state space $\N$ by
\[
  C_S\,i\,j \iff \big(i = 0 \wedge j+1 \in S\big) \ \vee\ i = j+1 .
\]
A positive state counts down deterministically; the base state $0$ may jump to $s-1$ for any nonzero $s \in S$, so that jumping and then descending is a closed computation at $0$ of length exactly $s$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Descent and rigidity]\label{lem:descent}
(i) $C_S^{(k)}\,k\,0$ for every $k$. (ii) If $C_S^{(k)}\,b\,0$ then $b \le k$ and $C_S^{(k-b)}\,0\,0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Induction on $k$ along the edges $k \to k-1$. (ii) Induction on $b$; for $b+1$ the only outgoing edge from the positive state $b+1$ goes to $b$, so apply the induction hypothesis to the tail.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Realisation Theorem]\label{thm:real}
For every $S \subseteq \N$, $\D(C_S,0) = \langle S\rangle$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\supseteq$) It suffices that $S \subseteq \D(C_S,0)$. For $s = 0$ this is trivial; for $s = j+1 \in S$ the edge $0 \to j$ followed by the descent of Lemma~\ref{lem:descent}(i) has length $j+1$.

($\subseteq$) Strong induction on $n$; $n=0$ is trivial. Let $n = j+1$ with a first edge $0 \to b$ followed by $C_S^{(j)}\,b\,0$. Since the source is $0$, the edge is of jump type, so $b+1 \in S$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:descent}(ii), $b \le j$ and $C_S^{(j-b)}\,0\,0$, so $j-b \in \langle S\rangle$ by induction. Then $n = (b+1) + (j-b) \in \langle S\rangle$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\D(C_M,0) = M$ for every additive submonoid $M \le \N$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Completeness]\label{cor:complete}
$\{\, M \le \N : \exists R,a,\ \D(R,a) = M\,\}$ is the entire lattice of additive submonoids of $\N$.
\end{corollary}

All four items of Example~\ref{ex:basic} are the instances $S = \varnothing, \{1\}, \{n\}, \{2,3\}$ of this one theorem --- and they exhaust the four qualitatively different regimes of the classification below.

\begin{corollary}[Lattice closure]
For any $R,S,a,b$ there are machines realising $\D(R,a)\cap\D(S,b)$ and $\D(R,a)\vee\D(S,b)$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Structure theory: period and gaps}\label{sec:structure}

\begin{definition}[Period]
$d(R,a) = \gcd \D(R,a)$, with the convention $\gcd\{0\} = 0$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Divisibility]
Every $n \in \D(R,a)$ is a multiple of $d(R,a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Structure theorem]\label{thm:struct}
There is $N$ such that every $m \ge N$ with $d(R,a) \mid m$ lies in $\D(R,a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose $m_1,\dots,m_r \in \D(R,a)$ with $\gcd(m_1,\dots,m_r) = d$. Every sufficiently large multiple of $d$ is a nonnegative integer combination of the $m_i$, e.g.\ by the coin-problem bound applied to the coprime numbers $m_i/d$.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Gaps]
$G(R,a) = \{ n : d(R,a) \mid n \ \wedge\ n \notin \D(R,a)\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{corollary}[Finiteness of gaps]
$G(R,a)$ is finite; indeed $G(R,a) \subseteq [0,N)$ for $N$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:struct}.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Dichotomy]
$d(R,a) = 0$ iff $\D(R,a) = \{0\}$. Otherwise $d(R,a) > 0$, all lengths are multiples of $d(R,a)$, and all sufficiently large multiples occur.
\end{theorem}

Up to the rescaling $n \mapsto n/d$, a nontrivial degree monoid is always a \emph{numerical semigroup}: a submonoid of $\N$ with finite complement.

\begin{theorem}[Synchronisation law]\label{thm:sync}
If $a$ and $b$ are live (each has a nonzero closed-computation length), then
\[
  d\big(R\times S,(a,b)\big) = \lcmop\big(d(R,a),\,d(S,b)\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Write $d_1,d_2$ for the periods and $L = \lcmop(d_1,d_2) > 0$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:prod} every element of the product's degree monoid is divisible by $d_1$ and $d_2$, hence by $L$; taking the gcd, $L$ divides the product's period. Conversely pick $N_1,N_2$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:struct} and $K > \max(N_1,N_2)$; then $Lk$ lies in the product's degree monoid for all $k \ge K$, in particular for $k = K$ and $k = K+1$, so the product's period divides their difference $L$. Conclude by antisymmetry of divisibility.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Chinese-remainder corollary]
Two single-loop machines of lengths $m$ and $n$ run in lockstep return to their common initial state exactly at the multiples of $\lcmop(m,n)$.
\end{corollary}

\section{Determinism}\label{sec:det}

\begin{definition}
$R$ is \emph{deterministic} if $R\,a\,b$ and $R\,a\,c$ imply $b = c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[Unique endpoints]\label{lem:unique}
If $R$ is deterministic then $R^{(n)}\,a\,b$ and $R^{(n)}\,a\,c$ imply $b = c$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $n$: the first edges agree by determinism, then apply the induction hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Subtraction closure]\label{thm:sub}
Let $R$ be deterministic and $m,n \in \D(R,a)$ with $m \le n$. Then $n-m \in \D(R,a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Split the $n$-loop at time $m$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:concat}): there is $b$ with $R^{(m)}\,a\,b$ and $R^{(n-m)}\,b\,a$. Since also $R^{(m)}\,a\,a$, Lemma~\ref{lem:unique} gives $b = a$, whence $R^{(n-m)}\,a\,a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Determinism forces a progression]\label{thm:prog}
If $R$ is deterministic then $\D(R,a) = d\N$ for a single $d$, namely the period $d(R,a)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $\D(R,a)$ has no nonzero element, take $d = 0$. Otherwise let $d$ be its least nonzero element; repeated addition gives $d\N \subseteq \D(R,a)$. Conversely, for $n \in \D(R,a)$ the multiple $d\lfloor n/d\rfloor$ lies in $\D(R,a)$ and is $\le n$, so by Theorem~\ref{thm:sub} the remainder $n \bmod d$ lies in $\D(R,a)$; being smaller than $d$, minimality forces it to vanish. Finally $\gcd(d\N) = d$.
\end{proof}

This is the Euclidean algorithm run inside the machine's own return times, made available by determinism.

\begin{corollary}[No gaps]
For deterministic $R$, $G(R,a) = \varnothing$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{corollary}[Gaps certify nondeterminism]
If $d(R,a) \mid n$ and $n \notin \D(R,a)$, then $R$ is not deterministic.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Separation]\label{thm:sep}
For no deterministic relation $R$ on any state space, and no state $a$, is $\D(R,a) = \langle 2,3\rangle$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Otherwise $\D(R,a) = d\N$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:prog}; from $2,3 \in \D(R,a)$ we get $d \mid \gcd(2,3) = 1$, so $\D(R,a) = \N \ni 1$, whereas $\langle 2,3\rangle = \{0\}\cup\{k : k\ge 2\}$ omits $1$.
\end{proof}

Thus finite nondeterministic machines realise every value of the invariant, while deterministic machines --- of any cardinality --- realise only the progressions $d\N$. The obstruction is arithmetic, not resource-theoretic.

\begin{theorem}[Period bound on finite state spaces]
Let $|\alpha| = N$, let $R$ be deterministic, and let $a$ be live. Then $d(R,a) \le N$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Put $d = d(R,a) > 0$, so $R^{(d)}\,a\,a$. For $i < d$ split the loop at time $i$ to get $s_i$ with $R^{(i)}\,a\,s_i$ and $R^{(d-i)}\,s_i\,a$. If $s_i = s_j$ with $i < j$, concatenating $R^{(i)}\,a\,s_i$ with $R^{(d-j)}\,s_j\,a$ yields a closed computation of length $i + (d-j)$, strictly between $0$ and $d$ --- impossible, as every nonzero length is a multiple of $d$. So $i \mapsto s_i$ is injective and $d \le N$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Finite-state realisation]\label{thm:finite}
Every additive submonoid $M \le \N$ is the degree monoid of a state of a machine with finitely many states.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Every submonoid of $\N$ is finitely generated; choose finite $T$ with $\langle T\rangle = M$ and put $B = \max T$. No transition of $C_T$ from a state $\le B$ leaves $\{0,\dots,B\}$, since jumps from the base go to $s-1 \le B-1$ and countdowns decrease. The inclusion $\{0,\dots,B\} \hookrightarrow \N$ is injective, preserves and reflects steps, and has image closed under transitions, so Theorem~\ref{thm:bisim} applies: the truncated machine has degree monoid $\langle T\rangle = M$ at its base, by Theorem~\ref{thm:real}.
\end{proof}

\section{Two-loop machines: the exact gap count}\label{sec:sylvester}

Fix coprime $p,q > 1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:real} the base state of $C_{\{p,q\}}$ has degree monoid the numerical semigroup $\langle p,q\rangle = \{ap+bq : a,b\in\N\}$, whose period is $\gcd(p,q) = 1$; the machine is aperiodic and its gap set is the finite complement $\N\setminus\langle p,q\rangle$.

\begin{lemma}[Existence of residues]
If $p > 0$ and $\gcd(q,p) = 1$, every $n$ admits $b < p$ with $bq \equiv n \pmod p$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Residue criterion]\label{thm:res}
Let $\gcd(p,q) = 1$ and let $b < p$ satisfy $bq \equiv n \pmod p$. Then $n \in \langle p,q\rangle$ iff $bq \le n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) $n - bq$ is a nonnegative multiple of $p$, say $ap$, so $n = ap+bq$. ($\Rightarrow$) If $n = a'p + b'q$ with $a',b'\ge 0$, then $b'q \equiv bq \pmod p$ and invertibility of $q$ modulo $p$ give $b' \equiv b \pmod p$; as $b < p$, we get $b' \ge b$, so $n \ge b'q \ge bq$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Frobenius number]\label{cor:frob}
$F := pq-p-q$ is the largest element of $\N \setminus \langle p,q\rangle$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since $pq - p \equiv 0 \pmod p$, we have $F \equiv -q \equiv (p-1)q \pmod p$, so the residue of $F$ is $p-1$; and $(p-1)q = pq-q > F$, so $F \notin \langle p,q\rangle$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:res}. If $n > F$ has residue $b \le p-1$ and $bq > n$, then $bq - n$ is a positive multiple of $p$, so $n \le bq - p \le (p-1)q - p = F$, a contradiction; hence $bq \le n$ and $n \in \langle p,q\rangle$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Symmetry]\label{thm:sym}
For $0 \le n \le F$, exactly one of $n$ and $F-n$ lies in $\langle p,q\rangle$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $b<p$ be the residue of $n$. As $F \equiv -q \pmod p$, we get $F - n \equiv -(b+1)q \pmod p$, so the residue of $F-n$ is $b' = p-1-b$, and
\[
  bq + b'q = (p-1)q = F + p .
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:res} it suffices to show exactly one of $bq \le n$, $b'q \le F-n$ holds. Both cannot hold: adding gives $F+p \le F$. Both cannot fail: then $bq-n$ and $b'q-(F-n)$ are positive multiples of $p$, hence each at least $p$, while their sum is $(bq+b'q)-F = p$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Sylvester's gap count]\label{thm:sylv}
For coprime $p,q>1$ the two-loop machine misses exactly
\[
  \#\big(\N\setminus\langle p,q\rangle\big) \;=\; \frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{2}
\]
computation lengths.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Corollary~\ref{cor:frob} all gaps lie in $\{0,\dots,F\}$, of cardinality $F+1 = (p-1)(q-1)$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:sym} the involution $n \mapsto F-n$ pairs each gap in this set with a non-gap, so exactly half are gaps.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
$(p,q) = (2,3)$: $F=1$, one gap (the length $1$) --- the certificate used in Theorem~\ref{thm:sep}. $(3,5)$: $F=7$, four gaps $1,2,4,7$. $(5,7)$: $F=23$, twelve gaps. $(7,11)$: $F=59$, thirty gaps.
\end{example}

\section{Algorithms}

\paragraph{Return-length spectrum by Boolean matrix powers.} For a machine on $N$ states with Boolean adjacency matrix $A$, $n \in \D(a)$ iff $(A^n)_{aa} = 1$; computing the spectrum up to length $L$ costs $O(LN^3)$ Boolean operations (or $O(LN^3/w)$ with bitset rows). The powers are eventually periodic, so a finite prefix determines the whole spectrum.

\paragraph{Period and gap extraction.} From a prefix, the period is the gcd of the observed nonzero lengths and the gaps are the absent multiples of it. By Theorem~\ref{thm:struct} the answer stabilises; by Theorem~\ref{thm:prog} any observed gap is a sound certificate of nondeterminism.

\paragraph{Membership and gap counting for $\langle p,q\rangle$.} Theorem~\ref{thm:res} decides membership in $O(\log p)$ arithmetic operations: compute $b = (q^{-1}n) \bmod p$ and compare $bq$ with $n$. Theorem~\ref{thm:sylv} counts the gaps in constant time.

\section{Discussion}

The degree monoid packages the temporal skeleton of a state, and Corollary~\ref{cor:complete} says it is complete for that data: beyond additivity and $0$-membership no universal constraint holds. Theorem~\ref{thm:sep} is a qualitative, absolute separation between deterministic and nondeterministic computation: $\langle 2,3\rangle$ is achieved by a three-state nondeterministic machine and by no deterministic machine at all. In the temporal dimension, determinism \emph{is} gaplessness. Finally the theory has an exact dictionary with numerical semigroups: coins correspond to loops, unpayable amounts to unachievable running times, the Frobenius number to the last unachievable time, and symmetry of the semigroup to a duality on the machine's timing diagram. The invariant is deliberately blind to everything but return times; its value lies in the totality of the classification within that narrow field of view.

\section{Future directions}\label{sec:future}

\paragraph{Determinisation cost.} Determinism forces $\D = d\N$, so a deterministic machine simulating a nondeterministic one must distort the invariant, and Theorem~\ref{thm:rescale} says how: rescaling by $k$ sends $M$ to $(M:k)$. Define the \emph{determinisation cost} $c(M)$ as the least $k_0$ such that $(M:k)$ is gapless for \emph{every} $k \ge k_0$; the uniform quantifier is needed because gaplessness for individual $k$ is erratic (e.g.\ $(\langle 3,5\rangle:3) = \N$ while $(\langle 3,5\rangle:4)$ still has the gap $1$).

\begin{proposition}
For coprime $p,q>1$ with $F = pq-p-q$ one has $c(\langle p,q\rangle) = F+1$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If $k > F$ then $kn > F$ for every $n \ge 1$, so $kn \in \langle p,q\rangle$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:frob} and $(\langle p,q\rangle:k) = \N$. Conversely, for $k = F \ge 1$ we have $1 \notin (\langle p,q\rangle:F)$ since $F \notin \langle p,q\rangle$, while $nF > F$ lies in $\langle p,q\rangle$ for $n \ge 2$; hence $(\langle p,q\rangle:F) = \{0,2,3,\dots\} = \langle 2,3\rangle$, which has period $1$ and the gap $1$.
\end{proof}

The reformulation turns ``speeding up a machine'' into a divisibility question inside the monoid lattice. Open: the value of $c(M)$ for a general numerical semigroup, and the structure of the erratic set $\{k : (M:k)\ \text{gapless}\}$ below the cost.

\paragraph{Relative invariants.} Replacing the base state by a pair $(a,b)$ and recording $\{n : R^{(n)}\,a\,b\}$ yields a module over $\D(R,a)$. The realisation problem for these relative invariants, and the corresponding determinism obstruction, is open and appears tractable by the same chain-machine technique.

\paragraph{Quantitative gap theory for many loops.} Sylvester's count is exact for two loops; for $r \ge 3$ generators the genus has no closed form, but machine-theoretic constraints (bounded state count, bounded out-degree) restrict which semigroups arise cheaply. Which numerical semigroups are realisable with at most $N$ states and out-degree at most $2$?

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from typing import List


def member(p: int, q: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Decide n in <p,q> for coprime p, q by the residue criterion."""
    if gcd(p, q) != 1:
        raise ValueError("p and q must be coprime")
    b = (pow(q, -1, p) * n) % p

    return p * q - p - q

    return (p - 1) * (q - 1) // 2

    """All unrealisable lengths, in O(F log p) time; there are (p-1)(q-1)/2."""
    F = frobenius_number(p, q)

    pos = sorted({g for g in gens if g > 0})

def cycle(n: int) -> Relation:

def product(r1: Relation, r2: Relation) -> Tuple[Relation, int]:

        nxt: Set[int] = set()
        for s in frontier:

        frontier = nxt
        if not frontier:

    return out


def period(lengths: Sequence[int]) -> int:
    d = 0
    for n in lengths:

  "interactive_layout": "# When Can a Machine Come Home? A Guided Tour of Return Times

Everything below is built from one deliberately crude measurement. Take any machine — a
controller, a protocol, a shuffling of a deck — put a stopwatch on one configuration $a$, and
record only the numbers of steps after which the machine can be at $a$ again. Call that set

$$D(a) \;=\; \{\, n \in \mathbb{N} : \text{$a$ can return to $a$ in exactly $n$ steps} \,\}.$$

By the end of this page you will know exactly which sets can occur, what they say about the
machine, and why one tiny missing number is a proof of nondeterminism.

---

## 1. Two facts you get for free

Doing nothing is a return of length $0$, so $0 \in D(a)$. And two returns can be run one after the
other, so if $m, n \in D(a)$ then $m + n \in D(a)$. That is all. In particular **you cannot
subtract**: being able to return in $5$ and in $2$ steps does not let you return in $3$.

A set of naturals containing $0$ and closed under addition is an *additive submonoid* of
$\mathbb{N}$. So the invariant is always algebra, never noise.

<details>
<summary><b>Why concatenation is the engine of the whole theory (click to expand)</b></summary>

Write $R^{(n)}\,a\,b$ for "$b$ is reachable from $a$ in exactly $n$ steps". The single fact that
everything below rests on is the *concatenation law*:

$$R^{(m+n)}\,a\,c \iff \exists b,\; R^{(m)}\,a\,b \ \wedge\ R^{(n)}\,b\,c .$$

Read left to right, it splits a long path at any intermediate time; read right to left, it glues
two paths. Gluing two loops at $a$ gives closure under addition. Splitting a loop at an
intermediate time is what will make determinism so powerful in §5 — for a deterministic machine
the state at that intermediate time is forced.

</details>

---

## 2. Play with it first

Before any theorems, build machines yourself. Toggle loop lengths; the panel paints every
computation length green if the machine can return in that many steps and **red** if it cannot,
even though the length is a multiple of the machine's period. Those red cells are called *gaps*,
and they are the entire subtlety of the subject.

Things worth trying:

* loops $\{2,3\}$ — a single red cell at $1$;
* loops $\{3,5\}$ — four red cells: $1,2,4,7$;
* loops $\{6,10\}$ — no red at all, just a clean period of $2$;
* loops $\{5,7\}$ — twelve red cells, the last at $23$; can you guess the formula before §6?
* then push the "speed-up factor" and watch the gaps evaporate.

## 3. Everything is possible: the Realisation Theorem

Is "additive submonoid" the *only* constraint? Yes — and the construction is a small machine you
can picture.

> **Chain machine.** Fix a set $S$ of loop lengths. States are $0,1,2,\dots$. A positive state $i$
> counts down to $i-1$; the base state $0$ may jump to $s-1$ for any $s \in S$. Jump-then-descend
> takes exactly $s$ steps and returns to $0$.

> **Realisation Theorem.** The base state of the chain machine of $S$ has
> $D(0) = \langle S\rangle$, the submonoid generated by $S$. Hence **every** additive submonoid of
> $\mathbb{N}$ is the return-time set of some state.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof sketch: why no other return times sneak in</b></summary>

One inclusion is the construction. For the other, note the machine is *rigid*: from a state $b$,
any path back to the base must spend at least $b$ steps counting down, and after those $b$ steps
it is at the base again. So a return of length $j+1$ begins with a jump of some length $b+1 \in S$
and continues with a shorter return, and strong induction finishes the argument.

</details>

Because every submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ is generated by a *finite* set, and the chain machine
never climbs above its largest generator, we can truncate:

> **Finite-state realisation.** Every additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ is the return-time set of
> a state of a machine with finitely many states.

## 4. The shape of the invariant: period and gaps

Define the **period** $d(a) = \gcd D(a)$.

* Every return time is a multiple of $d(a)$.
* All *sufficiently large* multiples of $d(a)$ are return times.
* Hence the gaps — multiples of the period that are not return times — are finitely many.
* $d(a) = 0$ happens exactly for a dead state, whose only return time is $0$.

Two machines running in lockstep intersect their invariants, so their periods combine by least
common multiple: two gears of $6$ and $10$ teeth realign every $30$ ticks. The atlas below shows
ten machines at once: every deterministic row is a flawless stripe, and every red cell in the
nondeterministic rows is — as the next section proves — impossible for any deterministic machine.

{{visualization:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>How the period and the gaps are actually computed from observations</b></summary>

You never need the transition table. Observe a prefix of the spectrum, take the gcd for the
period, and list the missing multiples. The structure theorem guarantees this stabilises.

## 5. The punchline: determinism *is* gaplessness

A machine is **deterministic** when each state has at most one successor.

> **Subtraction closure.** In a deterministic machine, if $m \le n$ are both return times then so
> is $n-m$.

Why: split the $n$-loop at time $m$. The state there is unique — and $a$ itself is one such state,
because $m$ is a return time. So the remaining $n-m$ steps form a loop at $a$.

Now run the Euclidean algorithm inside the machine's own return times:

> **Determinism forces an arithmetic progression.** For a deterministic machine,
> $D(a) = d\mathbb{N}$ exactly. Deterministic machines have **no gaps**.

Two consequences, and they are the reason this invariant is worth having:

> **Gaps certify nondeterminism.** One multiple of the period that is not a return time proves the
> machine is not deterministic — no need to find the branching state.

> **Separation Theorem.** No deterministic machine, on a state space of *any* size, has
> $\langle 2,3\rangle = \{0,2,3,4,\dots\}$ as its return-time set.

<details>
<summary><b>Three lines for the Separation Theorem</b></summary>

For a deterministic machine $D(a) = d\mathbb{N}$. If $2$ and $3$ are return times then $d \mid 2$
and $d \mid 3$, so $d = 1$ and $D(a) = \mathbb{N}$, which contains $1$. But $\langle 2,3\rangle$
does not contain $1$. The Frobenius gap $1$ is an intrinsic witness of nondeterminism.

</details>

Note what kind of statement this is. It is not a resource bound — the deterministic machine may
have infinitely many states, unbounded memory, anything at all. It is an obstruction of *shape*.
A useful reference point for the surrounding ideas is the classical theory of
[numerical semigroups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Numerical_semigroup) and the
[Frobenius coin problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coin_problem).

## 6. Counting the holes: Frobenius and Sylvester

Take two loops of coprime lengths $p, q > 1$. The return times are exactly the numbers
$ap + bq$ with $a,b \ge 0$ — the numerical semigroup $\langle p,q\rangle$, better known as the
Chicken McNugget problem.

**Residue criterion.** Since $q$ is invertible mod $p$, every $n$ has a unique $b \in [0,p)$ with
$bq \equiv n \pmod p$, and then
$$n \in \langle p,q\rangle \iff bq \le n.$$

**Frobenius number.** The largest gap is $F = pq-p-q$.

**Symmetry.** For $0 \le n \le F$, exactly one of $n$ and $F-n$ is a return time.

**Sylvester's count.** Therefore exactly half of the $F+1 = (p-1)(q-1)$ numbers in $[0,F]$ are
gaps:
$$\#\text{gaps} \;=\; \frac{(p-1)(q-1)}{2}.$$

<details>
<summary><b>The symmetry argument in full</b></summary>

Let $b$ be the residue of $n$. Since $F \equiv -q \pmod p$, the residue of $F-n$ is
$b' = p-1-b$, and
$$bq + b'q = (p-1)q = F + p.$$
Both inequalities $bq \le n$ and $b'q \le F-n$ cannot hold (adding gives $F+p \le F$). Both cannot
fail either: then $bq-n$ and $b'q-(F-n)$ are positive multiples of $p$, hence each at least $p$,
while their sum is exactly $p$. So exactly one holds, and the residue criterion converts this into
the claim.

</details>

## 7. Hiding nondeterminism by slowing down

Redefining one tick to mean $k$ steps replaces $M$ by the *colon monoid*
$(M:k) = \{n : kn \in M\}$. Since deterministic behaviour means gaplessness, we can ask how much
slowdown is needed before a machine's nondeterminism becomes invisible to the stopwatch. Define
the **determinisation cost** of $M$ as the least $k_0$ such that $(M:k)$ is gapless for *every*
$k \ge k_0$.

> For coprime $p,q>1$ the determinisation cost of $\langle p,q\rangle$ is exactly $F+1$, where
> $F = pq-p-q$: if $k > F$ then every $kn$ with $n\ge 1$ exceeds $F$ and is realisable, so the
> rescaled invariant is all of $\mathbb{N}$; whereas rescaling by $F$ itself yields
> $\{0,2,3,4,\dots\} = \langle 2,3\rangle$ — the canonical obstruction, gap and all.

/-- A transition relation is **deterministic** when each state has at most one successor. -/
def Deterministic (R : α → α → Prop) : Prop := ∀ a b c : α, R a b → R a c → b = c

/-- In a deterministic system a path of given length has a unique endpoint. -/
theorem iterR_unique {R : α → α → Prop} (hdet : Deterministic R) :

      exact ih x b c hxb hyc

/-- **Subtraction closure.**  The degree monoid of a state of a deterministic system is
closed under (truncated) subtraction. -/
theorem deterministic_sub_mem {R : α → α → Prop} (hdet : Deterministic R) {a : α} {m n : ℕ}

  have : b = a := iterR_unique hdet m a b a hb1 hm
  exact this ▸ hb2

# Degree monoids of abstract transition systems and the realisation theorem

An abstract computation is modelled by a *transition relation* `R : α → α → Prop`
on a state space `α`.  For a distinguished state `a` the set

  `{ n | a is reachable from a in exactly n R-steps }`

is the **degree monoid** `degreeMonoid R a`: it contains `0` and is closed under
addition, because two return loops can be concatenated (`iterR_add`).  It is the
basic *periodic invariant* of a state of a machine: the set of possible lengths
of computations that bring the machine back to the same configuration.

This file develops the theory:

* `iterR` — `n`-step reachability, with the concatenation law `iterR_add`;
* `degreeMonoid R a : AddSubmonoid ℕ` — the invariant;
* structural laws: monotonicity under simulations (`degreeMonoid_le_of_simulation`),
  invariance under bisimulation (`degreeMonoid_eq_of_bisim`), and the
  *product law* `degreeMonoid (prodRel R S) (a, b) = degreeMonoid R a ⊓ degreeMonoid S b`;
* the **realisation theorem** `degreeMonoid_chainRel`: the chain system generated by a set
  `S` of loop lengths has degree monoid `AddSubmonoid.closure S`, so *every* additive
  submonoid of `ℕ` occurs as a degree monoid (`degreeMonoid_chainRel_submonoid`).  Consequently the invariant is *complete*:
  the realisable set of degree monoids is exactly the lattice of additive
  submonoids of `ℕ` (`degreeMonoid_range`);
* the certified extremes and sample values: `⊥ = {0}`, `⊤ = ℕ`,
  `nℕ` (single-loop machine) and the numerical semigroup `⟨2,3⟩` (two-loop machine).

Everything is proved from scratch; no `sorry`, no `native_decide`.
-/
import Mathlib

namespace Computation
namespace DegreeMonoid

variable {α β : Type*}

/-! ## Exact-length reachability -/

/-- `iterR R n a b` says that `b` is reachable from `a` in **exactly** `n` steps of the
transition relation `R`. -/
def iterR (R : α → α → Prop) : ℕ → α → α → Prop
  | 0, a, b => a = b
  | n + 1, a, c => ∃ b, R a b ∧ iterR R n b c

@[simp] theorem iterR_zero (R : α → α → Prop) (a b : α) : iterR R 0 a b ↔ a = b := Iff.rfl

theorem iterR_succ (R : α → α → Prop) (n : ℕ) (a c : α) :
    iterR R (n + 1) a c ↔ ∃ b, R a b ∧ iterR R n b c := Iff.rfl

@[simp] theorem iterR_one (R : α → α → Prop) (a b : α) : iterR R 1 a b ↔ R a b := by
  simp [iterR_succ]

theorem iterR_refl (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : iterR R 0 a a := rfl

/-- **Concatenation law.**  A path of length `m + n` is a path of length `m` followed by a
path of length `n`.  This is the engine behind the monoid structure. -/
theorem iterR_add (R : α → α → Prop) (m n : ℕ) (a c : α) :
    iterR R (m + n) a c ↔ ∃ b, iterR R m a b ∧ iterR R n b c := by
  induction m generalizing a with
  | zero => simp
  | succ m ih =>
      rw [show m + 1 + n = (m + n) + 1 by ring, iterR_succ]
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨b, hab, hb⟩
        obtain ⟨c', h1, h2⟩ := (ih b).1 hb
        exact ⟨c', ⟨b, hab, h1⟩, h2⟩
      · rintro ⟨b, ⟨d, had, hdb⟩, hbc⟩
        exact ⟨d, had, (ih d).2 ⟨b, hdb, hbc⟩⟩

/-- Appending one step at the *end* of a path. -/
theorem iterR_succ' (R : α → α → Prop) (n : ℕ) (a c : α) :
    iterR R (n + 1) a c ↔ ∃ b, iterR R n a b ∧ R b c := by
  rw [iterR_add]; simp

/-! ## The degree monoid -/

/-- The **degree monoid** of a state: the set of lengths of closed computations at `a`.
It is an additive submonoid of `ℕ` by `iterR_add`. -/
def degreeMonoid (R : α → α → Prop) (a : α) : AddSubmonoid ℕ where
  carrier := {n | iterR R n a a}
  zero_mem' := iterR_refl R a
  add_mem' := by
    intro m n hm hn
    exact (iterR_add R m n a a).2 ⟨a, hm, hn⟩

@[simp] theorem mem_degreeMonoid {R : α → α → Prop} {a : α} {n : ℕ} :
    n ∈ degreeMonoid R a ↔ iterR R n a a := Iff.rfl

/-! ## Functoriality: simulations and bisimulations -/

/-- A map of state spaces that turns `R`-steps into `S`-steps transports closed
computations. -/
theorem iterR_map {R : α → α → Prop} {S : β → β → Prop} (f : α → β)
    (hf : ∀ a b, R a b → S (f a) (f b)) :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (a b : α), iterR R n a b → iterR S n (f a) (f b) := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero => rintro a b rfl; rfl
  | succ n ih =>
      rintro a c ⟨b, hab, hbc⟩
      exact ⟨f b, hf _ _ hab, ih _ _ hbc⟩

/-- **Simulation monotonicity.**  If `f` simulates `R` inside `S`, the degree monoid can
only grow. -/
theorem degreeMonoid_le_of_simulation {R : α → α → Prop} {S : β → β → Prop} (f : α → β)
    (hf : ∀ a b, R a b → S (f a) (f b)) (a : α) :
    degreeMonoid R a ≤ degreeMonoid S (f a) :=
  fun _n hn => iterR_map f hf _ _ _ hn

/-- **Bisimulation invariance.**  An injective simulation that also reflects steps
(and reflects the base state) preserves the invariant exactly. -/
theorem degreeMonoid_eq_of_bisim {R : α → α → Prop} {S : β → β → Prop} (f : α → β)
    (hinj : Function.Injective f)
    (hstep : ∀ a b, R a b ↔ S (f a) (f b))
    (hsurj : ∀ (a : α) (y : β), S (f a) y → ∃ b, f b = y)
    (a : α) : degreeMonoid R a = degreeMonoid S (f a) := by
  apply le_antisymm
  · exact degreeMonoid_le_of_simulation f (fun x y h => (hstep x y).1 h) a
  · intro n hn
    simp only [mem_degreeMonoid] at hn ⊢
    -- reflect an `S`-path through `f` back to an `R`-path
    have key : ∀ (n : ℕ) (x : α) (y : β), iterR S n (f x) y → ∃ z : α, f z = y ∧ iterR R n x z := by
      intro n
      induction n with
      | zero => intro x y hxy; exact ⟨x, hxy.symm ▸ rfl, rfl⟩
      | succ n ih =>
          rintro x y ⟨w, hw, hwy⟩
          obtain ⟨u, rfl⟩ := hsurj x w hw
          obtain ⟨z, hz, hz'⟩ := ih u y hwy
          exact ⟨z, hz, ⟨u, (hstep x u).2 hw, hz'⟩⟩
    obtain ⟨z, hz, hz'⟩ := key n a (f a) hn
    have : z = a := hinj hz
    exact this ▸ hz'

/-! ## Time rescaling: powers of a machine -/

/-- Iterating the `k`-step relation `n` times is the `k*n`-step relation: time rescaling. -/
theorem iterR_iterR (R : α → α → Prop) (k : ℕ) :
    ∀ (n : ℕ) (a b : α), iterR (fun x y => iterR R k x y) n a b ↔ iterR R (k * n) a b := by
  intro n
  induction n with
  | zero => intro a b; simp
  | succ n ih =>
      intro a b
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨c, hc, hrest⟩
        have : iterR R (k * n) c b := (ih c b).1 hrest
        have hcat : iterR R (k + k * n) a b := (iterR_add R k (k * n) a b).2 ⟨c, hc, this⟩
        have hk : k * (n + 1) = k + k * n := by ring
        rw [hk]
        exact hcat
      · intro h
        have hk : k * (n + 1) = k + k * n := by ring
        rw [hk] at h
        obtain ⟨c, hc, hrest⟩ := (iterR_add R k (k * n) a b).1 h
        exact ⟨c, hc, (ih c b).2 hrest⟩

degree monoid of the `k`-step machine is the `k`-th "colon monoid" of the original one. -/
theorem mem_degreeMonoid_pow (R : α → α → Prop) (k : ℕ) (a : α) (n : ℕ) :
    n ∈ degreeMonoid (fun x y => iterR R k x y) a ↔ k * n ∈ degreeMonoid R a := by
  simpa using iterR_iterR R k n a a

/-! ## Products: the invariant is a lattice meet -/

/-- Synchronous product of two transition systems. -/
def prodRel (R : α → α → Prop) (S : β → β → Prop) : α × β → α × β → Prop :=
  fun p q => R p.1 q.1 ∧ S p.2 q.2

theorem iterR_prodRel (R : α → α → Prop) (S : β → β → Prop) (n : ℕ) (p q : α × β) :
    iterR (prodRel R S) n p q ↔ iterR R n p.1 q.1 ∧ iterR S n p.2 q.2 := by
  induction n generalizing p with
  | zero =>
      constructor
      · rintro rfl; exact ⟨rfl, rfl⟩
      · rintro ⟨h1, h2⟩
        exact Prod.ext h1 h2
  | succ n ih =>
      constructor
      · rintro ⟨r, hr, hrest⟩
        obtain ⟨h1, h2⟩ := (ih r).1 hrest
        exact ⟨⟨r.1, hr.1, h1⟩, ⟨r.2, hr.2, h2⟩⟩
      · rintro ⟨⟨x, hx, hx'⟩, ⟨y, hy, hy'⟩⟩
        exact ⟨(x, y), ⟨hx, hy⟩, (ih (x, y)).2 ⟨hx', hy'⟩⟩

/-- **Product law.**  The degree monoid of a synchronous product is the intersection of the
degree monoids of the factors: the invariant turns products of machines into meets of
submonoids. -/
theorem degreeMonoid_prodRel (R : α → α → Prop) (S : β → β → Prop) (a : α) (b : β) :
    degreeMonoid (prodRel R S) (a, b) = degreeMonoid R a ⊓ degreeMonoid S b := by
  ext n
  simpa using iterR_prodRel R S n (a, b) (a, b)

/-! ## The chain system realising an arbitrary submonoid -/

/-- The **chain system** generated by a set `S ⊆ ℕ` of loop lengths.  States are natural
numbers; a positive state `i` counts down deterministically (`i → i - 1`), while the base
state `0` may jump to `s - 1` for any nonzero `s ∈ S`, i.e. it enters a loop of length
exactly `s`. -/
def chainRel (S : Set ℕ) : ℕ → ℕ → Prop :=
  fun i j => (i = 0 ∧ j + 1 ∈ S) ∨ i = j + 1

/-- From state `k` the machine reaches the base in exactly `k` steps. -/
theorem chainRel_descend (S : Set ℕ) : ∀ k : ℕ, iterR (chainRel S) k k 0 := by
  intro k
  induction k with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ k ih => exact ⟨k, Or.inr rfl, ih⟩

/-- Every path from a state `b` to the base state has length at least `b`, and its tail of

theorem chainRel_path_to_base (S : Set ℕ) :
    ∀ (b k : ℕ), iterR (chainRel S) k b 0 → b ≤ k ∧ iterR (chainRel S) (k - b) 0 0 := by
  intro b
  induction b with
  | zero => intro k hk; exact ⟨Nat.zero_le k, by simpa using hk⟩
  | succ b ih =>
      intro k hk
      cases k with
      | zero => exact absurd hk (by simp)
      | succ j =>
          obtain ⟨c, hc, hrest⟩ := hk
          have hcb : c = b := by
            rcases hc with ⟨h0, _⟩ | h
            · exact absurd h0 (Nat.succ_ne_zero b)
            · omega
          subst hcb
          obtain ⟨hle, hzero⟩ := ih j hrest
          refine ⟨by omega, ?_⟩
          simpa [Nat.succ_sub_succ] using hzero

of `ℕ` is generated by itself, *every* submonoid is realised: the invariant is complete. -/
theorem degreeMonoid_chainRel (S : Set ℕ) :
    degreeMonoid (chainRel S) 0 = AddSubmonoid.closure S := by

            have hbS : b + 1 ∈ S := by

            have hmem : (j - b) ∈ AddSubmonoid.closure S := ih (j - b) (by omega) hzero

theorem degreeMonoid_chainRel_submonoid (M : AddSubmonoid ℕ) :
    degreeMonoid (chainRel (M : Set ℕ)) 0 = M := by
  rw [degreeMonoid_chainRel, AddSubmonoid.closure_eq]

            lengths.append(n)
        frontier = step_set(rel, frontier)
        if not frontier:
            break
    return lengths


def is_submonoid_prefix(lengths: Sequence[int], horizon: int) -> bool:
    """Check 0 in D and closure under addition, as far as the horizon allows."""
    members = set(lengths)
    if 0 not in members:
        return False
    for m, n in product(lengths, repeat=2):
        if m + n <= horizon and (m + n) not in members:
            return False
    return True


def period(lengths: Iterable[int]) -> int:
    """gcd of the closed-computation lengths (0 for the dead state)."""
    d = 0
    for n in lengths:
        d = gcd(d, n)
    return d


def gaps(lengths: Sequence[int], horizon: int) -> List[int]:
    """Multiples of the period, up to the horizon, that are not realised."""
    d = period(lengths)
    members = set(lengths)
    if d == 0:
        return []
    return [m for m in range(0, horizon + 1, d) if m not in members]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Machine constructions
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def chain_machine(generators: Sequence[int], top: int | None = None) -> Relation:
    """The chain machine of a set S of loop lengths.

    States 0..B where B = max(S) (or `top`). A positive state i steps to i-1;
    the base 0 may jump to s-1 for each nonzero s in S. Jump-then-descend is a
    closed computation at 0 of length exactly s.
    """
    pos = [s for s in generators if s > 0]
    bound = top if top is not None else (max(pos) if pos else 0)
    rel: Relation = {i: set() for i in range(bound + 1)}
    for i in range(1, bound + 1):
        rel[i].add(i - 1)
    for s in pos:
        rel[0].add(s - 1)
    return rel


def cycle_machine(n: int) -> Relation:
    """A single deterministic cycle of length n >= 1."""
    return {i: {(i + 1) % n} for i in range(n)}


def synchronous_product(r1: Relation, r2: Relation) -> Tuple[Relation, Dict[Tuple[int, int], int]]:
    """Synchronous product; returns the relation and the state encoding."""
    states = [(a, b) for a in r1 for b in r2]
    code = {p: i for i, p in enumerate(states)}
    rel: Relation = {code[p]: set() for p in states}
    for (a, b) in states:
        for a2 in r1.get(a, set()):
            for b2 in r2.get(b, set()):
                rel[code[(a, b)]].add(code[(a2, b2)])
    return rel, code


def rescale(rel: Relation, k: int) -> Relation:
    """The k-step machine: one new tick = k old steps."""
    out: Relation = {}
    for s in rel:
        frontier: Set[State] = {s}
        for _ in range(k):
            frontier = step_set(rel, frontier)
        out[s] = frontier
    return out


def is_deterministic(rel: Relation) -> bool:
    return all(len(succ) <= 1 for succ in rel.values())


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Numerical semigroup utilities
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def in_two_generator_semigroup(p: int, q: int, n: int) -> bool:
    """Residue criterion: with b = q^{-1} n mod p, membership iff b*q <= n."""
    b = (pow(q, -1, p) * n) % p
    return b * q <= n


def frobenius_number(p: int, q: int) -> int:
    return p * q - p - q


def sylvester_gap_count(p: int, q: int) -> int:
    return (p - 1) * (q - 1) // 2


def brute_force_gaps(p: int, q: int) -> List[int]:
    limit = frobenius_number(p, q) + 1
    return [n for n in range(limit + 1) if not in_two_generator_semigroup(p, q, n)]


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Demonstrations
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------
def banner(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 74)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 74)


def demo_monoid_law(horizon: int = 40) -> None:
    banner("1. The degree monoid is an additive submonoid of N")
    catalogue = {
        "dead state (no transitions)": {0: set()},
        "self-loop": {0: {0}},
        "4-cycle": cycle_machine(4),
        "two loops of lengths 2 and 3": chain_machine([2, 3]),
        "three loops of lengths 4, 6, 9": chain_machine([4, 6, 9]),
    }
    for name, rel in catalogue.items():
        spec = degree_spectrum(rel, 0, horizon)
        print(f"{name:32s} D = {spec[:12]}{' ...' if len(spec) > 12 else ''}")
        assert is_submonoid_prefix(spec, horizon), name
        print(f"{'':32s} period = {period(spec)}, gaps = {gaps(spec, horizon)}")
    print("\nAll listed spectra contain 0 and are closed under addition.")


def demo_realisation(horizon: int = 60) -> None:
    banner("2. Realisation: the chain machine of S realises <S>")

    def generated_prefix(gens: Sequence[int], horizon: int) -> List[int]:
        reachable = [False] * (horizon + 1)
        reachable[0] = True
        for n in range(horizon + 1):
            if reachable[n]:
                for g in gens:
                    if g > 0 and n + g <= horizon:
                        reachable[n + g] = True
        return [n for n in range(horizon + 1) if reachable[n]]

    for gens in ([], [1], [5], [2, 3], [3, 5], [4, 6, 9], [6, 10, 15]):
        rel = chain_machine(gens)
        observed = degree_spectrum(rel, 0, horizon)
        expected = generated_prefix(gens, horizon)
        ok = observed == expected
        print(f"S = {str(gens):14s} states = {len(rel):3d}  matches <S>: {ok}")
        assert ok
        print(f"{'':17s}D = {observed[:14]}{' ...' if len(observed) > 14 else ''}")


def demo_products(horizon: int = 80) -> None:
    banner("3. Product law: intersection of monoids, lcm of periods")
    for m, n in ((4, 6), (3, 5), (6, 10), (2, 3)):
        r1, r2 = cycle_machine(m), cycle_machine(n)
        prod, code = synchronous_product(r1, r2)
        spec_prod = degree_spectrum(prod, code[(0, 0)], horizon)
        s1 = set(degree_spectrum(r1, 0, horizon))
        s2 = set(degree_spectrum(r2, 0, horizon))
        inter = sorted(s1 & s2)
        L = m * n // gcd(m, n)
        print(f"cycles {m} x {n}: D(product) = {spec_prod[:8]}"
              f"  intersection = {inter[:8]}  lcm = {L}  period = {period(spec_prod)}")
        assert spec_prod == inter
        assert period(spec_prod) == L


def demo_rescaling(horizon: int = 40) -> None:
    banner("4. Rescaling law: D(R^[k], a) = { n : k*n in D(R,a) }")
    for gens, k in (([2, 3], 2), ([3, 5], 3), ([6], 2), ([4, 6, 9], 2)):
        rel = chain_machine(gens)
        base_spec = set(degree_spectrum(rel, 0, k * horizon))
        fast = rescale(rel, k)
        observed = degree_spectrum(fast, 0, horizon)
        expected = [n for n in range(horizon + 1) if k * n in base_spec]
        print(f"S = {str(gens):12s} k = {k}:  D = {observed[:10]}   predicted = {expected[:10]}")
        assert observed == expected
        print(f"{'':20s} gaps before rescaling: {gaps(sorted(base_spec), 20)}, "
              f"after: {gaps(observed, 20)}")


def demo_determinism(horizon: int = 60) -> None:
    banner("5. Determinism <=> gaplessness")
    examples = {
        "5-cycle (deterministic)": cycle_machine(5),
        "chain machine of {6} (deterministic loop)": chain_machine([6]),
        "two loops 2,3 (nondeterministic)": chain_machine([2, 3]),
        "two loops 3,5 (nondeterministic)": chain_machine([3, 5]),
    }
    for name, rel in examples.items():
        spec = degree_spectrum(rel, 0, horizon)
        d = period(spec)
        g = gaps(spec, horizon)
        det = is_deterministic(rel)
        print(f"{name:44s} deterministic = {str(det):5s} period = {d}  gaps = {g}")
        if det:
            assert g == [], "a deterministic machine must be gapless"
        if g:
            assert not det, "a gap certifies nondeterminism"
    print("\nSeparation: <2,3> = {0,2,3,4,...} has the gap 1 at period 1,")
    print("so no deterministic machine on any state space realises it.")


def demo_frobenius_sylvester() -> None:
    banner("6. Frobenius number and Sylvester's gap count")
    print(f"{'(p,q)':>10} {'F = pq-p-q':>12} {'#gaps':>8} {'(p-1)(q-1)/2':>14}   gaps")
    for p, q in ((2, 3), (3, 5), (4, 7), (5, 7), (7, 11), (5, 12)):
        if gcd(p, q) != 1:
            continue
        g = brute_force_gaps(p, q)
        F = frobenius_number(p, q)
        assert max(g) == F
        assert len(g) == sylvester_gap_count(p, q)
        shown = g if len(g) <= 10 else g[:10] + ["..."]
        print(f"{str((p, q)):>10} {F:>12} {len(g):>8} {sylvester_gap_count(p, q):>14}   {shown}")

    print("\nSymmetry check: for 0 <= n <= F exactly one of n, F-n is realisable.")
    for p, q in ((3, 5), (5, 7), (7, 11)):
        F = frobenius_number(p, q)
        ok = all(in_two_generator_semigroup(p, q, n)
                 != in_two_generator_semigroup(p, q, F - n) for n in range(F + 1))
        print(f"  (p,q) = ({p},{q}), F = {F}: involution n -> F-n swaps gaps and non-gaps: {ok}")
        assert ok


def demo_machine_vs_criterion(horizon: int = 80) -> None:
    banner("7. Machine simulation agrees with the residue criterion")
    for p, q in ((2, 3), (3, 5), (5, 7)):
        rel = chain_machine([p, q])
        spec = set(degree_spectrum(rel, 0, horizon))
        predicted = {n for n in range(horizon + 1) if in_two_generator_semigroup(p, q, n)}
        print(f"(p,q) = ({p},{q}): simulated spectrum equals residue criterion: {spec == predicted}")
        assert spec == predicted


def demo_finite_state_bound() -> None:
    banner("8. Finite-state realisation and the deterministic period bound")
    for gens in ([2, 3], [3, 5], [4, 6, 9], [5, 12]):
        rel = chain_machine(gens)
        print(f"S = {str(gens):12s} realised by a machine with {len(rel)} states "
              f"(max generator + 1 = {max(gens) + 1})")
        assert len(rel) == max(gens) + 1
    print("\nDeterministic machines on N states have period <= N:")
    for n in (3, 5, 8):
        rel = cycle_machine(n)
        spec = degree_spectrum(rel, 0, 3 * n)
        print(f"  {n}-cycle: states = {len(rel)}, period = {period(spec)} <= {len(rel)}")
        assert period(spec) <= len(rel)


def main() -> None:
    demo_monoid_law()
    demo_realisation()
    demo_products()
    demo_rescaling()
    demo_determinism()
    demo_frobenius_sylvester()
    demo_machine_vs_criterion()
    demo_finite_state_bound()
    print("\nAll demonstrations completed successfully.")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
"
  },

    "Catalog/Speculative/AutoResearch/DegreeMonoidRealisation.lean",
    "Catalog/Speculative/AutoResearch/DegreeMonoidStructure.lean",
    "Catalog/Speculative/AutoResearch/DegreeMonoidDeterminism.lean",
    "Catalog/Speculative/AutoResearch/DegreeMonoidSylvester.lean"
  ]
}

# Phase A Research Mission v19c: General codiscrete construction

            ## Assignment
            **Domain**: Combinatorics | **Mode**: team
            **Description**: Package the construction for every unital magma, proving that codiscrete hom-categories turn arbitrary unit and associativity defects into coherent invertible 2-cells.
            **Mathematical Framing**: Package the construction for every unital magma, proving that codiscrete hom-categories turn arbitrary unit and associativity defects into coherent invertible 2-cells.



            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

ADDITIONALLY — machine-readable directions block (REQUIRED). In
FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md, after the prose sections, emit a fenced JSON
array named future_directions.json with one object per direction
(3–6 entries), each with exactly these keys:
```json
[{"title": "<short noun-phrase name, NOT a sentence>",
  "domain": "<one of: NumberTheory, Algebra, Geometry, Combinatorics, Computation, Physics, Probability, Cryptography, Logic, MachineLearning, Tropical, Bridges>",
  "description": "<2-4 sentences: the conjecture, the approach, why it matters>",
  "conjecture": "<the precise mathematical claim>",
  "test": "<how to test or formalize it>",
  "if_true": "<consequence if true>",
  "if_false": "<consequence if false>",
  "proof_strategy": "<sketch of the proof route>",
  "catalog_references": ["<Catalog.lean.module>"]}]

Titles must be noun phrases ("Silver-Ratio Spectral Gap for Pell Spines"),
never sentences or recaps ("This cycle proved..." is forbidden).

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the

concept.title: Definability boundary for external interpretations
concept.concept_description:
**Conjecture.** An external interpretation is recoverable from structural truth exactly when it is constant on automorphism orbits and definable in the invariant language; for finite models, orbit constancy alone is sufficient after adding bounded counting modalities.

The key insight is that the meaning-collision example fails precisely because the interpretation does not factor through structural equivalence, suggesting orbit descent as the necessary condition and definability as the sufficient one.

**Why now?** The collision theorem provides the negative half of a classification problem, while finite orbit decompositions offer a direct route to testing the proposed converse.
